questions.question: A 48-year-old male with a history of recurrent childhood otitis media and chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction presents with persistent malodorous, purulent left ear discharge and progressive hearing loss for 18 months. Otoscopy reveals a deep retraction pocket in the posterosuperior pars flaccida with erosion of the scutum and cheesy, foul-smelling keratinaceous debris. Pure-tone audiogram confirms a 42 dB conductive hearing loss in the left ear. Tympanometry reveals a flat tracing with an equivalent ear canal volume of 3.2 mL (normal reference: 0.6– 1.5 mL). What is the diagnosis, the expected tympanogram type, and the definitive treatment?

options.A: Primary acquired cholesteatoma; Tympanogram: Type B with abnormally large ear canal volume (>2.0 mL); Treatment: Tympanomastoidectomy (surgical eradication)
options.B: Otitis media with effusion (OME); Tympanogram: Type B with normal ear canal volume; Treatment: Oral antihistamines and decongestants alone
options.C: Acute suppurative otitis media; Tympanogram: Type A; Treatment: High-dose oral amoxicillin for 10 days
options.D: Otosclerosis; Tympanogram: Type As; Treatment: Stapedectomy with piston placement
options.E: Keratosis obturans; Tympanogram: Type Ad; Treatment: Topical antifungal drops

questions.explanation:
This patient presents with Primary Acquired Cholesteatoma complicating chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction and otitis media.
• Pathogenesis: Chronic negative middle ear pressure pulls the flaccid pars flaccida into Prussak's space, creating an invaginated retraction pocket. Desquamated keratin accumulates, undergoes secondary infection with Pseudomonas or Proteus (causing foul-smelling otorrhea), and secretes osteolytic enzymes (collagenases, acid phosphatase, TNF-alpha) that erode adjacent ossicles (incus long process) and the bony scutum.
• Tympanometry Interpretation: A flat tracing (no compliance peak) with an abnormally large equivalent ear canal volume (>2.0–2.5 mL) represents a Type B tympanogram where the probe air volume includes both the external canal AND the middle ear/mastoid cavity due to a tympanic membrane perforation or eroded open attic pocket.
• In contrast, Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) produces a Type B tympanogram with normal canal volume (0.6–1.5 mL).
• Definitive Management: Tympanomastoidectomy (canal-wall-up or canal-wall-down) to completely resect the matrix, aerate the middle ear, and reconstruct the ossicular chain.

HIGH-YIELD: Type B Tympanogram Volume Distinction (Crucial Board Concept):
• Type B + Normal Volume (0.6–1.5 mL): Middle ear fluid / intact drum (Otitis Media with Effusion).
• Type B + Large Volume (>2.0–2.5 mL): Perforated TM, patent tympanostomy tube, or large eroded cholesteatoma pocket.
• Type B + Small Volume (<0.5 mL): Occluded probe tip, impacted cerumen, or severe canal stenosis.

EXAM TRAP: Foul-smelling (fetid) chronic ear drainage that does not respond to topical or oral antibiotic therapy is a cholesteatoma until proven otherwise. Immediate referral for CT and mastoidectomy is required.

optionExplanations.A:
Correct. This patient presents with Primary Acquired Cholesteatoma complicating chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction and otitis media.
• Pathogenesis: Chronic negative middle ear pressure pulls the flaccid pars flaccida into Prussak's space, creating an invaginated retraction pocket. Desquamated keratin accumulates, undergoes secondary infection with Pseudomonas or Proteus (causing foul-smelling otorrhea), and secretes osteolytic enzymes (collagenases, acid phosphatase, TNF-alpha) that erode adjacent ossicles (incus long process) and the bony scutum.
• Tympanometry Interpretation: A flat tracing (no compliance peak) with an abnormally large equivalent ear canal volume (>2.0–2.5 mL) represents a Type B tympanogram where the probe air volume includes both the external canal AND the middle ear/mastoid cavity due to a tympanic membrane perforation or eroded open attic pocket.
• In contrast, Otitis Media with Effusion (OME) produces a Type B tympanogram with normal canal volume (0.6–1.5 mL).
• Definitive Management: Tympanomastoidectomy (canal-wall-up or canal-wall-down) to completely resect the matrix, aerate the middle ear, and reconstruct the ossicular chain.
optionExplanations.B: OME causes amber fluid without bone erosion or foul odor, and its Type B curve has NORMAL ear canal volume.
optionExplanations.C: AOM is an acute febrile infection with an intact bulging drum, not an 18-month osteolytic attic process.
optionExplanations.D: Otosclerosis has a normal TM, Type As tympanogram, and is treated with stapedectomy.
optionExplanations.E: Keratosis obturans is confined to the external bony auditory canal without tympanic membrane retraction or scutum erosion.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose acquired cholesteatoma, interpret a Type B tympanogram with large equivalent canal volume, and identify tympanomastoidectomy as definitive surgical treatment.
